context.heading: Kept, kept, kept
context.body: Jude keeps returning to tēreō ("keep"). Believers are "kept" in Jesus Christ (v. 1); rebel angels did not keep their domain and are now kept in chains (v. 6); darkness is kept for the false teachers (v. 13); and believers must keep themselves in God's love (v. 21). The same word marks both God's protection and His judgment.

context.heading: Slipping in through a side door
context.body: The false teachers "crept in unnoticed" (pareisdunō), a word for slipping in sideways past a guard. They were insiders, eating at the church's love feasts (v. 12). Their error was moral as much as doctrinal: they turned grace into aselgeia, unrestrained indulgence, and so denied Jesus as Master.

context.heading: Quoting Enoch
context.body: Verses 14–15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9, a Jewish writing from before Christ that was widely read but not part of the Hebrew Bible. Verse 9 likely draws on a tradition preserved in a work often called the Assumption of Moses. Quoting a book does not make all of it Scripture, much as Paul quotes pagan poets (Acts 17:28); Jude affirms this particular prophecy as true.

theology.title: Judgment with a long memory
theology.body: Jude gives three Old Testament warnings: Israel rescued from Egypt yet judged in the wilderness (Numbers 14), angels who abandoned their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19). Interpreters differ on whether the angels refer to Genesis 6:1–4 or to an earlier rebellion. The point is the same: privilege never exempts anyone from God's justice.

theology.title: Jesus, Lord of the Exodus
theology.body: Jesus is "our only Master and Lord" (v. 4), and despotēs ("Master") is used of God Himself in Luke 2:29 and Acts 4:24. Several important early manuscripts of verse 5 say it was Jesus who delivered Israel out of Egypt, while others read "the Lord." Either way, Jude places the Son alongside the God who saved Israel (compare 1 Corinthians 10:4).

theology.title: Able to keep you from stumbling
theology.body: The letter ends in worship, not anxiety. The God who keeps rebels for judgment is able to keep His people from stumbling and present them amōmos ("unblemished"), a word for a sacrificial animal without defect (v. 24). Glory belongs to Him through Jesus Christ before all time, now and forever (v. 25).

application.title: Grace is not a loophole
application.body: The false teachers turned God's grace into permission for whatever they wanted (verse 4). The same move happens whenever "God will forgive me" becomes the reason to go ahead. Grace that never changes your direction has been misunderstood.
application.question: Where have you used God's forgiveness as a reason to keep going rather than to stop?

application.title: Contending without contempt
application.body: Even the archangel Michael would not hurl insults at the devil but left the rebuke to the Lord (verse 9). Jude calls believers to fight for the faith while showing mercy to doubters and pulling others from the fire (verses 22–23). Conviction and compassion are both commanded.
application.question: In arguments about faith or politics, do you sound more like Michael or like the scoffers?

application.title: Impressive from a distance
application.body: Clouds without water and trees without fruit (verse 12) look promising until you need them. Jude's test for leaders is what they produce and whom they serve, since these men were shepherding only themselves. Charisma is not the same as fruit.
application.question: Which voices do you follow because they look impressive rather than because their lives bear fruit?
